name: People Pleaser Test
tagline: Find out how much you bend to keep others happy.
intro: This test looks at four sides of people-pleasing: needing approval, struggling with boundaries, neglecting your own needs and avoiding conflict. Answer based on how often each statement fits you in daily life. It takes about five minutes and helps you see where kindness to others may come at a cost to yourself.
seoTitle: People Pleaser Test: Free online self-check
seoDescription: Are you a people pleaser? Take this 5-minute test on approval, boundaries, self-neglect and conflict avoidance and get practical tips for healthier habits.

approval.name: Need for approval
approval.short: How much your sense of worth depends on others liking you.
approval.low: Your answers suggest you feel fairly secure, even when not everyone approves of you. You seem able to share your views and make your own choices without constant reassurance. This independence makes your relationships more honest. Keep staying open to feedback, though: listening to people you trust remains valuable. Just continue to weigh it against your own values rather than letting it decide for you.
approval.mid: Your answers suggest that other people's approval matters to you quite a bit in some situations. You may feel secure with close friends but adapt yourself more at work or with new people. Notice when you change an opinion or hide a preference just to be liked. Try sharing one honest preference a day, even a small one like where to eat. Each time, observe that relationships usually survive honesty well.
approval.high: Your answers suggest that your sense of worth leans strongly on what others think of you. You may feel anxious when someone seems displeased and work hard to keep everyone happy. This can be very tiring and can make it hard to know what you really want. Start by listing qualities you value in yourself that do not depend on praise. Practise tolerating small moments of disapproval. If this pattern affects your wellbeing, a qualified professional such as a therapist can help you build steadier self-worth.

boundaries.name: Weak boundaries
boundaries.short: How hard it is for you to say no and protect your time and limits.
boundaries.low: Your answers suggest you are good at saying no and protecting your time. You seem able to set limits without long explanations or heavy guilt. Healthy boundaries make it easier to help others with genuine energy. Keep checking that your limits stay flexible enough for the people and causes that really matter to you, so firmness does not turn into distance.
boundaries.mid: Your answers suggest you can set boundaries, but not always. Some people or situations probably make it harder to say no, for instance a demanding boss or a close friend. Try using a pause phrase such as "Let me check and get back to you" before agreeing. This gives you time to decide what you really want. Notice which requests drain you most and practise declining those first.
boundaries.high: Your answers suggest you often say yes when you want to say no, and others may take up more of your time and energy than feels right. Over time this can lead to exhaustion and resentment. Start small: decline one low-stakes request this week with a short, friendly sentence and no long excuse. Remind yourself that a clear no is also a kindness. If you feel unable to set limits or feel taken advantage of, a qualified professional can support you in building healthier boundaries.

self_neglect.name: Self-neglect
self_neglect.short: How often you put your own needs, rest and goals last.
self_neglect.low: Your answers suggest you take good care of your own needs while still caring for others. You seem to make time for rest, hobbies and personal goals, and you can accept help. This balance protects you from burnout and lets you give to others from a full tank. Keep it up by planning regular time for yourself, especially during busy periods when it is most tempting to skip it.
self_neglect.mid: Your answers suggest that your own needs sometimes slip down the list, particularly when others need you. You may still look after yourself, but not always consistently. Try scheduling one activity a week that is only for you and treat it like an appointment. When someone offers help, practise simply saying thank you and accepting it. Small acts of self-care add up over time.
self_neglect.high: Your answers suggest you often put yourself last, skipping rest, hiding your problems or letting your own goals slide. This can leave you tired, overlooked and quietly resentful. Your needs matter as much as anyone else's. Begin by noticing one need each day, such as rest, food or company, and meet it before helping someone else. Ask one person for help with something small. If you feel drained or low, please consider talking to a doctor or a qualified professional.

conflict_avoidance.name: Conflict avoidance
conflict_avoidance.short: How strongly you avoid disagreements and difficult conversations.
conflict_avoidance.low: Your answers suggest you handle disagreements fairly comfortably. You seem able to raise issues, give honest feedback and stand up for yourself without too much stress. This helps problems get solved early. Keep combining directness with warmth, and remember to listen as carefully as you speak, so that conflicts stay constructive and relationships grow stronger through them. Choosing your moment well also helps.
conflict_avoidance.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes avoid conflict, especially when the stakes feel high or the other person matters a lot to you. Small irritations may build up before you mention them. Try raising issues while they are still small, using a calm "I" sentence such as "I felt overlooked when…". Prepare one key point beforehand. Most disagreements become easier once they are out in the open.
conflict_avoidance.high: Your answers suggest you go to great lengths to avoid conflict, even when it costs you. You may stay silent, take the blame or agree just to keep the peace. In the long run this can harm both your wellbeing and your relationships, because problems stay unsolved. Practise expressing small disagreements in safe situations first. Remember that healthy conflict is normal. If tension or anger around you causes strong anxiety, a qualified professional can help you feel safer speaking up.

summary: People-pleasing is not one single habit but a mix of patterns. Below you see how strongly four of them show up in your answers. Higher scores mean more people-pleasing in that area. Caring about others is a strength; the goal is balance, not becoming less kind. This is a self-reflection tool, not a diagnosis.
